displayName: Bill Watterson

properties.note: Creator, and sole author and artist of every strip; born 1958.

displayName: First strip

properties.note: Published in 35 newspapers; the strip then ran daily until 1995.

displayName: Last strip

properties.note: Sunday strip: Calvin and Hobbes sled downhill into the snow.

displayName: Universal Press Syndicate

properties.note: Syndicated the strip; United Feature Syndicate first declined it.

displayName: Andrews McMeel Publishing

properties.note: Publishes the collected books.

displayName: Eighteen book collections

properties.note: Published 1987-1997; eleven of them archive every daily strip.

displayName: The Complete Calvin and Hobbes

properties.note: Three hardback volumes, 1,440 pages, released 4 October 2005; a four-volume paperback followed in 2012.

displayName: More than 2,000 newspapers

properties.note: Peak international circulation of the daily strip.

displayName: Humor, family life, philosophy, satire

properties.note: The genres the strip is usually described by.

displayName: Angouleme Grand Prix

properties.note: Awarded to Watterson in 2014, the fourth American after Eisner, Crumb and Spiegelman.

displayName: No official merchandise

properties.note: Watterson refused to license the characters, and the strip was never made into an animation.

displayName: Calvin

properties.note: Six-year-old protagonist, named after the theologian John Calvin; striped shirt, spiky blond hair.

displayName: Hobbes

properties.note: Calvin's stuffed tiger: real to Calvin, a toy to everyone else. Named after Thomas Hobbes and modelled on Watterson's cat Sprite.

displayName: Mom

properties.note: Calvin's unnamed stay-at-home mother, usually exhausted; she is the one who curbs his worst impulses.

displayName: Dad

properties.note: Calvin's unnamed father, a patent attorney and outdoorsman, modelled on Watterson's own father.

displayName: Susie Derkson

properties.note: Calvin's classmate and neighbour; polite, diligent and usually Calvin's equal in cunning. The surname appears as both Derkson and Derkins in sources.

displayName: Mr. Bun

properties.note: Susie's stuffed rabbit; never shown as a living character, and once described as comatose.

displayName: Miss Wormwood

properties.note: Calvin's strict teacher, named after the apprentice demon in C. S. Lewis' The Screwtape Letters. Calvin is back in her class every autumn.

displayName: Moe

properties.note: Calvin's school bully, drawn in crude lower-case letters; the only major character never portrayed sympathetically.

displayName: Rosalyn

properties.note: The last major recurring character to appear: a high-school senior, and the only baby-sitter Calvin fears.

displayName: Uncle Max

properties.note: Calvin's father's older brother; he appeared in a series of 1988 strips and never came back.

displayName: Calvin's grandparents

properties.note: Mentioned in strips: a grandfather who complains that comic strips are printed too small, and a grandmother Calvin plays cards with.

displayName: Amy

properties.note: Another baby-sitter Calvin's parents hired; she has apparently purged him from her memory.

displayName: Charlie

properties.note: Rosalyn's unseen boyfriend, whose arrangements she repeatedly cancels by telephone.

displayName: Principal Spittle

properties.note: Calvin's school principal, seen over his desk while Calvin explains himself; he hates his job.

displayName: Mr. Lockjaw

properties.note: Gym teacher and coach of the school baseball team; he lets Moe's violence pass and calls Calvin a quitter.

displayName: Mr. Kneecapper

properties.note: The only substitute teacher Calvin's class is given a name for.

displayName: Maurice

properties.note: One of the two named monsters under Calvin's bed.

displayName: Winslow

properties.note: The other named monster under Calvin's bed.

displayName: Pete

properties.note: The barber Calvin visits once; barbers named Charlie and others are also mentioned.

displayName: Calvin's doctor

properties.note: Calvin's mild-mannered pediatrician, whom Calvin imagines as a vicious interrogator.

displayName: Susie's mom

properties.note: Shown only from the waist down, in a foiled attempt to pester Susie.

displayName: Spaceman Spiff

properties.note: Calvin's astronaut, an explorer of the galaxy whose deserts are based on southern Utah; the idea grew out of Watterson's earlier Spaceman Mort.

displayName: Tracer Bullet

properties.note: A hardboiled private eye drawn in shadowy film-noir black and white; he appeared when Calvin wore a fedora to hide a haircut.

displayName: Stupendous Man

properties.note: A superhero whose mask and cape Calvin's mother made, and who narrates his own adventures.

displayName: Calvin's cardboard box

properties.note: A corrugated box Calvin sits in: the recurring device that turns any object or situation into an adventure, from time travel to self-duplication.

displayName: Transmogrifier

properties.note: Calvin's device for turning its user into any creature or object.

displayName: Duplicator

properties.note: Calvin's machine for copying himself; he once modified it to copy only his good side.

displayName: Invisible Cretinizer

properties.note: Calvin's pretend gadget for making other people invisible.

displayName: Wagon and sled rides

properties.note: The downhill rides Calvin and Hobbes take in every season; Watterson used them to break up talking heads and to let Calvin think aloud.

displayName: Calvin's snowmen

properties.note: Calvin builds snowmen with avant-garde forms; they are the main vehicle for his parodies of the art world.

displayName: Calvinball

properties.note: Improvised game invented in 1990 after Calvin's bad spell in the school baseball team. Rules are made up as you go, never the same twice, and every player wears a mask.

displayName: G.R.O.S.S.

properties.note: Get Rid Of Slimy girlS: Calvin and Hobbes's club, run from the treehouse, with Calvin as Dictator-for-Life and Hobbes as President-and-First-Tiger.

displayName: Horrendous Space Kablooie

properties.note: Calvin's alternative name for the Big Bang theory, coined in a Sunday strip of 21 June 1992 and often shortened to the HSK.

displayName: Imagination versus reality

properties.note: Calvin's inner world is real to him and Hobbes lives in it; Watterson never settles which of the two readings is truer.

displayName: Philosophical banter

properties.note: Calvin and Hobbes argue about determinism, morality, the meaning of life and the future, usually at each other's expense.

displayName: Parents who do not know

properties.note: Mom and Dad are outmatched, exasperated and occasionally at a loss; Watterson said they parent Calvin better than he would.

displayName: School as an institution

properties.note: Homework, tests, Show and Tell and Miss Wormwood's class, against which Calvin declares war of attrition.

displayName: Greed and consumerism

properties.note: Allowances, cookies, presents and fund-raising letters: Calvin treats money as a tool for acquiring happiness.

displayName: The failed future

properties.note: Flying cars, moon colonies and personal robots never arrive, and Hobbes doubts our ability to manage the technology already invented.

displayName: Nature is indifferent

properties.note: The outdoors ignores Calvin; he argues with it about fear, awe, science and frogs.

displayName: Winter and snow

properties.note: Snow, sledding and snow goons: Calvin's snowmen and his best and worst behaviour.

displayName: Sport and losing

properties.note: Baseball, Calvinball, and the lesson that competition only divides people into winners and losers.

displayName: Avant-garde art

properties.note: Calvin's snowmen and drawings as cutting-edge art, defended with the jargon of art criticism.

displayName: Death and the afterlife

properties.note: What happens when we die, whether God and the Devil exist, and how to live anyway.

displayName: Food as currency

properties.note: Cookies, frozen goods and meals traded and hoarded; Calvin treats the kitchen as a commodity.

displayName: Pop psychobabble

properties.note: Calvin justifies his rampages with pseudo-psychological jargon such as toxic codependency.

displayName: Civics and polls

properties.note: Calvin polls his father, wants to vote while refusing to follow issues, and writes fund-raising letters built on antagonism.

displayName: Science and doubt

properties.note: Newton's first law, why ice floats, the Big Bang, and the strip's own punchline that the answers are boring.
